course_description:
Written communication remains a fundamental aspect of work in all professions. Despite the rise of digital alternatives, effective writing is still a vital skill for anyone seeking employment in the 21st century workplace. This course covers key theoretical principles and practical applications of writing in a corporate environment.

To get, keep and advance in any job, you'll need to be able to write effectively. This is far more complex than simply being able to generate grammatically-standard sentences -- effective workplace writing relies on your ability to gather and assess information, and apply it to your local context; to communicate expert information in a way that's usable for a wide range of audiences; to write in and adapt to specific genres and voices; and to collaborate with others.

Employers consistently report that these writing skills are among their highest priorities when hiring graduates, and that many graduates are not well-prepared to write in their jobs.

WRIT2000 sets you up to perform in your profession, focussing on hands-on, practical strategies to enhance the content, quality and style of your workplace writing.

Over the course of the semester, we'll cover key workplace genres including reports, evaluations, presentations and job applications, as well as principles for effective writing that you can apply to other genres. In lecture, we'll focus on the key concepts that underpin workplace writing practices; in tutorials, we'll practice applying those principles in hands-on, interactive writing exercises that will develop your skills over time and prepare you to complete your assessment tasks.

Because this is a practical class, regularly attending and participating in tutorial activities is critical to your success in the course, including your capacity to complete your at-home writing tasks.

By completing this course, you will develop the confidence and competence to write effectively and continue developing as a writer throughout your career.

course_aims: This course aims to prepare students for the literacy demands of the service-oriented workplace.

learning_outcomes.description: understand the functional and situational nature of writing in the professional workplace
be familiar with the conventions, styles and formats of the most common professional communications
be able to generate, evaluate, analyse, synthesise, and organise information, using problem-solving strategies
have the skills to create specific professional documents that are accessible to a wide range of readers
understand how professional writing and editing works and be able to take responsibility for your ongoing development as writer/editors in the professions for which you are preparing.

assessment_details.task_description: You'll collaborate with a small group of classmates to produce minutes for one of your tutorial meetings and present the minutes for class endorsement in the next meeting. This assessment is in two parts, both assessed pass/fail: the team-authored minutes (10%) and an individually-authored team evaluation (5%). Signups will happen in the Week 4 tutorial meeting, when your team will develop your team charter together. The first set of minutes will be taken in the Week 5 tutorial meeting (presented in Week 6), and the last set in Week 12 (presented in Week 13). Preparing for and participating in your group is part of the requirements for this task. If you fail to enrol in a group or if you do not participate adequately in your agreed group, you cannot be added to a/another group at a later stage as this would disadvantage other team members. In this scenario, you will earn a 0 for this assessment item. Full details, including the marking criteria and standards, are in the Assessments folder on Blackboard. learning_activities.topic: Week 1: Course introduction Introduction to the course and the principles of writing for pay.
Week 1: Class orientation Writing activities and discussion.
Week 2: User-centred communication Identifying and addressing target users.
Week 2: Writing usable documentation Writing activities and discussion.
Week 3: No Lecture-Public Holiday Public holiday Wednesday 12/8/26.
Week 3: No Tutorial-Public Holiday Public holiday Wednesday 12/8/26.
Week 4: Ethics and accountability Writing for and with others: ethics, accountability and relationality in workplace writing.
Week 4: Minutes team formation & 1st team meeting Minutes assignment sign-ups. Team writing exercises.
Week 5: Correspondence Emails, letters and memos.
Week 5: Writing effective emails Email-writing activities. Minutes assignment continues.
Week 6: Technical writing Technical writing, including definitions and descriptions. Minutes assignment begins (first team taking minutes, to be presented and endorsed in Week 5).
Week 6: Writing descriptions Description-writing activities. Minutes assignment continues.
Week 7: Verbal communication Writing for audio delivery: presentations, speeches and interviews.
Week 7: Presenting expert information Powerpoint Party. Minutes assignment continues.
Week 8: Reports Writing and designing reports.
Week 8: Writing reports Report-writing activities. Minutes assignment continues.
Week 9: Persuasive writing Writing advice and warnings that promote action.
Week 9: Writing PSAs Advice-writing activities. Minutes assignment continues.
Mid-Semester Break No class meetings this week.
Week 10: No Lecture (King's Birthday holiday 5/10/26) No class meetings this week. Public holiday Monday 5/10/26.
Week 10: No Tutorial (King's Birthday holiday 5/10/26) No class meetings this week. Public holiday Monday 5/10/26.
Week 11: Job applications Job application materials: CVs, resumes, selection criteria responses, cover letters.
Week 11: Writing CVs CV-writing activities. Minutes assignment continues.
Week 12: Document design Document design and structure.
Week 12: Design and data communication Design and data communication exercises. Minutes assignment continues (last group taking minutes, to be presented in Week 13).
Week 13: Wrap-up and next steps Synthesis and application of the entire course.
Week 13: Writing selection criteria responses Undertake "Selection criteria response" assessment. Minutes assignment concludes (presentation and endorsement of Week 12 minutes).

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
